questions.q: What table is the legacy Workflow Editor built on?
options: sys_hub_flow
wf_workflow
sys_hub_action_type_definition
sysapproval_approver
questions.explain: The Workflow Editor's graphical canvas is built on the wf_workflow table — ServiceNow's original automation tool, predating Flow Designer.

questions.q: Why did the Workflow Editor's canvas get difficult to work with on complex automation?
options: It only supported a single activity per workflow
It required a separate license for every activity added
Activities often needed JavaScript, and the canvas could get visually tangled with more than a handful of branches
It could not be used for approvals of any kind
questions.explain: The Workflow Editor is a genuinely developer-oriented model — configuring activities often meant writing script, and tracing execution order meant following lines across an increasingly tangled canvas.

questions.q: What table is Flow Designer built on, and what release era did ServiceNow begin promoting it as the recommended tool?
options: wf_workflow, starting around Helsinki
sys_hub_flow, starting around Kingston/London
sys_hub_action_type_definition, starting around Madrid
sysapproval_approver, starting around Geneva
questions.explain: Flow Designer runs on sys_hub_flow, and ServiceNow has promoted it as the recommended automation tool since roughly the Kingston/London releases.

questions.q: Why has ServiceNow left legacy Workflow running instead of forcing all instances to migrate to Flow Designer?
options: Legacy Workflow is actually faster to execute than Flow Designer
Flow Designer cannot replicate approval logic
An automatic, forced migration would risk breaking existing production automation across many customer instances
ServiceNow has not yet built a way to create new flows
questions.explain: Both tools coexist deliberately: legacy Workflows keep running as built, while Flow Designer is where new automation gets built, avoiding the risk of breaking production automation through a forced migration.

questions.q: What does this course expect you to be able to do with the legacy Workflow Editor, specifically?
options: Build new multi-step Workflows from scratch as your primary skill
Recognize it by name and table, and be able to read an existing one well enough not to break it — building new automation happens in Flow Designer
Nothing — legacy Workflow is never encountered on real instances
Convert every legacy Workflow to Flow Designer automatically using a built-in migration button
questions.explain: This course teaches Flow Designer exclusively for building; reading an existing legacy Workflow well enough not to break it is a real-world skill picked up on the job, not a separate building skill taught here.
